definition: Retrievability is a term associated with the ease with which information can be found or retrieved using an information system, specifically a search engine or information retrieval system.
details: A document (or information object) has high retrievability if there are many queries which retrieve the document via the search engine, and the document is ranked sufficiently high that a user would encounter the document. Conversely, if there are few queries that retrieve the document, or when the document is retrieved the documents are not high enough in the ranked list, then the document has low retrievability. Retrievability can be considered as one aspect of findability. Applications of retrievability include detecting search engine bias, measuring algorithmic bias, evaluating the influence of search technology, tuning information retrieval systems and evaluating the quality of documents in a collection. Retrievability is also key to the process of Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) - a technique that enables large language models (LLMs) to retrieve and incorporate new information. RAG is used whenever AI needs to select information from a private corpus or any source it hasn't been trained on. Agentic AI web browsing applications also depend heavily on the retrievability of website content.

explainer.lead: Retrievability describes how easily a document can actually be found through a search engine. It matters because a document nobody's query surfaces is effectively invisible, even if it exists.

tiers.eli5: A book buried at the back of a library with no catalogue entry is hard to find, while one listed under many subjects gets found easily.
tiers.practitioner: Engineers judge retrievability by how many queries return a document and how high it ranks, treating it as one aspect of findability. A pitfall is optimizing ranking while ignoring how few queries reach the document at all.
tiers.paperLevel: A document has high retrievability if many queries retrieve it via the search engine and it is ranked sufficiently high for a user to encounter it; low if few queries retrieve it or it ranks too low. It is an aspect of findability; the definition gives no single numeric formula.

explainer.example: A page returned for many related queries and ranked near the top has high retrievability; one returned for one obscure query far down the list has low retrievability.
